recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what each part factorises into and what cancels.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Factorise both parts
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both parts vanish at x = 3, so (x − 3) is a factor of each. Split the middle term of the numerator: −8x = −3x − 5x.
steps.memory_tip: Both parts are zero at x = 3, so (x − 3) must divide both. Look for it before doing anything else.
lines: Putting x = 3 gives (9 − 24 + 15)/(9 − 9) = 0/0, so both parts are factorised.

recall.must_convey: That the numerator is (x − 3)(x − 5) and the denominator is (x − 3)(x + 3).

steps.why: The 0/0 form is caused by the factor (x − 3) sitting in both parts. Factorising is what brings that shared factor into the open so it can be removed; nothing can be substituted until it is gone.
common_mistakes: Splitting the middle term as −4x − 4x, which does not give the product 15.
Writing x² − 9 as (x − 3)², which is x² − 6x + 9.

steps.label: Cancel (x − 3) and substitute
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Say x ≠ 3 before cancelling — a limit at 3 never uses the value at 3, which is what makes the cancelling legal.
steps.memory_tip: Cancel first, substitute second. Substituting before cancelling gives 0/0 again.
lines: As x → 3 we have x ≠ 3, so (x − 3) may be cancelled:

recall.must_convey: That (x − 3) cancels since x ≠ 3, and substituting x = 3 gives −2/6 = −1/3.

steps.why: A limit as x → 3 only looks at values of x other than 3, so (x − 3) is not zero and may be divided out. Once it is gone the remaining expression is defined at 3 and direct substitution is valid.
common_mistakes: Cancelling without saying x ≠ 3, which reads as dividing by zero.
Leaving the answer as −2/6 instead of reducing it to −1/3.
